content: Axillary hair, commonly referred to as underarm hair, is the hair that grows in the underarm region. This type of hair typically begins to develop during puberty and usually completes its growth by the end of adolescence. The release of pheromones from the axillary region during this stage of human development suggests a potential link between underarm hair and human sexuality. In mammals, the olfactory response to pheromones and the subsequent enhancement of sexual drive provide insights into the possible purpose and significance of axillary hair in humans. It has also been proposed that underarm hair serves a functional role by reducing friction between the upper arm and the thorax. In contemporary society, particularly in many Western countries, it is more common for women than men to regularly remove their underarm hair for aesthetic reasons. This practice may be related to the general distribution of body hair between the sexes. However, the prevalence of underarm hair removal varies significantly across cultures. Some Western women choose to leave their underarm hair as a statement of defiance against societal norms. In contrast, in certain Eastern European countries and in China, underarm shaving is less common and is not considered a necessary aesthetic practice. In Islamic culture, both men and women often remove underarm hair as part of personal cleanliness and religious observance. While underarm hair provides a larger surface area for bacteria to thrive, the use of deodorants and antiperspirants has largely mitigated these concerns. Competitive swimmers often remove all body hair, including underarm hair, to reduce drag and improve performance, while bodybuilders frequently do so for aesthetic purposes. The practice of underarm hair removal in the Western world began around 1915 in the United States and the United Kingdom, when magazines featured women in sleeveless dresses with shaved underarms. The introduction of the safety razor in the early 20th century made regular shaving more practical. While underarm shaving quickly gained popularity in English-speaking countries, particularly in the U.S. and Canada, it did not become widespread in continental Europe until after World War II. There is a common misconception that shaving hair causes it to grow back thicker over time. However, shaving does not create new hair follicles or alter the thickness of the hair. This myth likely persists because shaved hair lacks the natural taper of longer hair, making it feel coarser, and because stubble appears darker and more noticeable. Underarm hair grows faster than leg hair, necessitating more frequent removal. Over time, the underarm area may darken, and even with a close shave, a shadow may remain visible. Since hair beneath the skin can contribute to this dark appearance, waxing, which removes hair from the root, can effectively reduce underarm darkness.
